task.goal: Design a recurring shared reading ritual for residents of a small apartment building that works even if only a few people participate.
hard_constraints: A committee has a lobby shelf, paper and four weeks; no resident directory, app or public ranking.
Do not collect identifiable reading histories or require book purchases.
Participation must remain optional and accessible to residents who cannot stand at the shelf; define a two-week feasibility pilot.
task.available_resources: Donated public-domain short texts and volunteer check-ins.
task.expected_result: A repeatable ritual, privacy safeguards and observable pilot checks.

DIRECT_FULL.title: One passage, one weekly pause
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make one short passage the building’s shared weekly reference point. Each Monday, volunteers place paper copies of a donated public-domain text on the lobby shelf, with one optional question such as “Which image stayed with you?” Residents can read whenever they wish. At a fixed weekly time, a volunteer offers a ten-minute read-aloud and conversation; one resident and one volunteer are enough, and silence is welcome. Reading alone still counts as participating.

The mechanism is a predictable shared focus: residents can encounter the same words without coordinating schedules or finishing a book. It assumes a volunteer can keep the appointment and that at least one suitable seated location is available. For residents unable to reach or stand at the shelf, volunteers offer paper delivery or an individual read-aloud during existing, consented check-ins. The committee must confirm this access route before launching; it cannot assume every resident already receives visits.

Use the first week to choose four short texts, prepare a plain-language invitation and confirm accessibility. Pilot during weeks two and three; use week four to adjust the routine. Invitations should say that attendance, comments and future contact are optional. Keep no names, quotations attributed to residents, attendance lists or records of who reads which text. Any temporary delivery arrangements stay with the volunteer and are discarded when no longer needed. This requires paper, shelf space and dependable volunteer time. Its limit is that a shared passage may create familiarity without producing conversation.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: For the two-week pilot, offer one passage and one scheduled pause each week. Also leave an equally short, unprompted public-domain text available as a simple shelf-only comparator. At optional check-ins, ask whether the scheduled shared passage gave residents a reason to read or connect that the unprompted text did not. Record only broad operational findings, without linking answers across weeks. Check that copies and read-aloud access reached anyone requesting them, and that the appointment happened even with one participant. If residents find the schedule burdensome or see no additional value, retain the simpler shelf-only option.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A paper conversation that waits for you
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Create a weekly conversation carried by paper rather than simultaneous attendance. Put copies of one short public-domain text on the shelf alongside a folded response sheet. Its outside carries one concrete prompt; inside, residents may leave an unsigned sentence, a drawing or a question. A volunteer checks the sheet midweek and adds a response grounded in the text when needed, so a single resident can receive an answer. At week’s end, the volunteer places a brief, unattributed recap beside the next text.

The mechanism is delayed reciprocity: someone encounters a previous response and can answer it without meeting its author. It assumes residents are comfortable with contributions being visible to neighbours and that a volunteer can moderate twice weekly. Do not promise anonymity: handwriting or personal anecdotes may identify someone. Invite text-focused contributions, discourage personal details, and state that identifying or hurtful material will be removed. Do not copy or archive original sheets; discard them after the weekly recap. Participation requires neither a contribution nor a purchase.

During week one, prepare two texts, response sheets and the privacy notice. Run the pilot in weeks two and three, then revise in week four. Residents unable to stand at or reach the shelf can receive copies through consented volunteer check-ins, dictate a text-focused response for transcription, and hear the previous contributions read aloud. Volunteers must obtain permission before sharing dictated words. No directory or ongoing reader profiles are created. This needs paper, pencils and a volunteer willing to respond and moderate. Its limits are possible reluctance to write publicly and the risk that volunteer contributions dominate.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: In each pilot week, offer the conversation sheet alongside an ordinary take-away copy of the same text. Inspect whether any resident contribution receives a relevant reply, including a volunteer reply, and whether later contributions engage with earlier ones. Keep only a weekly aggregate description, not individual records or handwriting samples. Ask willing participants whether reading others’ responses added anything beyond the plain copy and whether privacy felt adequate. If neither week produces reciprocal engagement, or residents avoid the sheet because of exposure concerns, the mechanism has not justified its extra work.

DIRECT_FULL.title: The next instalment belongs to next week
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Turn a short public-domain story into a recurring two-part reading. Each fortnight, residents receive the first half in week one and the conclusion in week two. Choose a text with a natural break and label the release dates clearly. Include a short recap with the conclusion so residents can join late. Offer one optional prompt before the ending arrives: “What do you think happens next?” Residents can consider it privately or discuss it during a volunteer check-in; no predictions are collected or scored.

The mechanism is narrative anticipation. An unfinished story supplies a reason to return, while a common release rhythm gives even two neighbours an easy conversation starter. Unlike a discussion meeting, the ritual does not depend on residents attending together. It assumes the committee can find a short, readable story whose division feels enjoyable rather than frustrating. State its approximate reading time. Residents who prefer the complete story may request both halves immediately; the weekly rhythm must never become a condition of access.

Use week one of the committee’s four weeks to select and prepare a story and confirm accessible distribution. Run its two instalments during weeks two and three, then decide in week four whether to repeat fortnightly. Put paper copies on the shelf and offer delivery or read-aloud versions through consented volunteer check-ins for residents unable to stand there. Volunteers keep no records of reading progress or predictions; any temporary delivery instructions are discarded after use. Resources are two paper batches, a short recap and volunteer availability. The main limits are unsuitable story breaks, memory demands and residents simply preferring complete texts.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: During the two-week pilot, make a complete-story packet available alongside the dated instalments. At optional check-ins, ask whether waiting for the ending created pleasant anticipation, caused frustration or made no difference compared with receiving the whole story. Inspect whether the second instalment was released reliably and whether residents joining in week two could follow it using the recap. Record only aggregate operational observations and unattributed feedback themes. If willing readers consistently prefer the complete packet, or the recap does not support late entry, abandon serial release and use complete texts.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Pass the editor’s turn
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Give residents a small, consequential editorial role: choosing what the building reads next. Each week, a volunteer prepares two donated public-domain passages, each complete and short enough to read in about five minutes. An optional resident editor chooses one and gives it a text-focused invitation, such as “Read this for its surprising last sentence.” The volunteer prints that invitation with the passage. Everyone may read privately, discuss it during a consented check-in, or simply take a copy. No meeting or written response is required.

The mechanism is shared ownership: a neighbour’s editorial choice gives an otherwise ordinary shelf text a local reason to be read. One willing resident can sustain the role with volunteer support; if nobody chooses, the volunteer supplies the next selection. Editors may repeat, and residents need never disclose their role publicly. This assumes someone enjoys choosing and that volunteers can offer two genuinely accessible options. It may fail if choosing feels like homework or volunteer selections dominate.

Use week one to prepare four candidate passages and a paper invitation explaining how to request an editorial turn through a volunteer check-in. Run the two-week pilot in weeks two and three; use week four to revise or stop. Provide large, clear print and offer delivery, oral presentation of the choices, and read-aloud access through explicitly consented check-ins. Confirm a workable request route for residents unable to reach or stand at the shelf before launch.

Keep no editor roster, reading histories, names on passages, or public tally. Invitations must avoid personal anecdotes that identify the chooser. Volunteers retain delivery instructions only as long as needed. Resources are paper, shelf space, prepared texts and brief volunteer visits; no purchases, directory or app are needed.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: In each pilot week, offer the resident-selected passage beside an equally short volunteer-selected passage, clearly labelled by selection method without naming anyone. Reverse their shelf positions in week two. During optional check-ins, ask whether the neighbour’s choice supplied any extra reason to read and whether choosing felt enjoyable or burdensome. Do not track who takes either passage or link feedback across weeks. Record only whether selection and accessible distribution happened, plus broad feedback themes; suppress details that could identify a lone participant. The mechanism lacks support if nobody wants an editorial turn, choosing creates pressure, or willing readers find the neighbour-selected invitation adds nothing over the ordinary selection. Two weeks can establish feasibility, not lasting participation.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Read, notice, return
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make reading the start of a small noticing practice. Each week, offer one complete public-domain passage and an optional invitation drawn from it: after a description of light, notice one change in daylight; after a passage about listening, attend to an ordinary sound. The following week’s sheet opens with “Bring last week’s observation to mind,” then introduces a new passage and practice. Nothing must be reported, written or completed.

The mechanism is transfer into everyday life: a passage becomes a recurring cue for attention, giving residents a shared activity between readings. Two residents can follow the same practice without meeting; one can participate meaningfully alone. This differs from sustaining interest through discussion or an unfinished story. Its central assumption is that the invitation makes reading more resonant rather than turning it into homework.

In preparation week one, volunteers select two short texts and devise invitations that require no purchases, travel, physical exertion or particular sensory ability. Offer alternatives such as noticing, recalling or imagining. Run the two-week pilot in weeks two and three; use week four to revise the format. Continue weekly only if the practice adds value.

Keep copies on the lobby shelf. Through consented volunteer check-ins, offer seated delivery and individual read-aloud access, including an oral explanation of the practice. Before launch, establish an accessible way to request this help without relying solely on a shelf notice. Participation and conversation remain optional.

Resources are paper, suitable donated texts and brief volunteer preparation and check-ins. Collect no observations, names, completion records or reading histories. Do not display participation totals. The main limits are prompts feeling prescriptive and texts becoming secondary to the activity.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: For each pilot passage, provide a plain version and a version with the noticing invitation. During optional check-ins, ask whether the invitation helped the passage stay meaningful, added a burden or made no difference; residents need not disclose what they noticed. Check that both weekly releases and requested accessible formats were delivered. Retain only nonidentifying operational findings, omitting distinctive anecdotes. If willing residents find the plain reading equally useful or prefer it because the activity feels obligatory, the added mechanism is unsupported. Two weeks tests usability, not lasting benefit.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Read the same words two ways
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Build a weekly ritual around a second encounter with the same complete passage. Each sheet offers two short reading passes: first read normally; then choose a different lens, such as attending to sounds rather than events, or imagining how a minor character understands the scene. Finish by privately considering whether anything changed. A volunteer can demonstrate the two passes aloud during an optional check-in. No interpretation is collected or judged.

The mechanism is perceptual variation: a familiar text can produce a fresh experience without requiring more material, another participant or a conversation. Residents share the same experiment in attention, while differing responses remain private. A single participant can sustain the ritual. It assumes that the selected passage rewards another reading and that instructions are understandable without literary expertise.

Use week one to prepare two complete, brief public-domain passages, each with one concrete alternative lens. Avoid school-like questions, correct answers and demands to perform aloud. Pilot one passage per week during weeks two and three, then use week four to simplify or discontinue the format. Repeat weekly with a new passage if residents find the second encounter worthwhile.

Paper copies remain available on the shelf. Confirm an accessible invitation and request route before launch; consented volunteer check-ins can provide delivery, seated reading or both readings aloud. Residents may choose either pass, stop midway or simply take the plain text. No purchase, meeting or written response is required.

This needs paper, modest text preparation and volunteers able to read without testing residents. Keep no attendance lists, attributed interpretations or records of who tried which lens. Any delivery arrangements remain temporary and separate from feedback. The main risks are repetition feeling tedious and the ritual resembling an assessment.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Offer each pilot text with a detachable or separately supplied second-pass instruction, leaving the plain passage usable alone. At optional check-ins, ask whether another ordinary reading or the suggested lens would be preferable, and whether the lens revealed anything worthwhile without requiring residents to explain their interpretation. Inspect whether instructions can be understood without extended coaching and whether read-aloud access works. Retain only broad, nonidentifying findings. If the lens consistently confuses readers, feels evaluative or adds nothing beyond ordinary rereading, remove it. With very little feedback, report feasibility as uncertain.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Choose what today needs
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Create a recurring reading ritual that begins with a private intention rather than a shared assignment. Each week, place three complete, short public-domain passages on the shelf under modest invitations such as “For a little amusement,” “For close attention” and “For a moment of wonder.” Residents silently choose whatever appeals, read it and privately consider whether it suited the moment. They may choose several or none. Use the same invitations each week with fresh texts.

The mechanism is relevance at the point of choice: selecting an intended experience may make reading easier to begin and easier to return to. The building shares a recognizable ritual without requiring everyone to read the same passage. It works with a handful of residents because its value does not depend on contributions or attendance. It assumes volunteers can find texts that plausibly fit the invitations; these are reading suggestions, not promises about emotional or health outcomes.

During week one, prepare two weekly sets using available donated texts. Keep passages complete and brief, with clear print and descriptive headings. Run the two-week pilot in weeks two and three; review in week four. Future sets can reuse texts, limiting preparation demands.

Before launch, confirm an accessible way to learn about and request the selection. During consented volunteer check-ins, offer all three passages together for seated delivery, or read the options aloud and provide the resident’s choice. No explanation of a choice is requested. Residents can also ask for a passage without choosing an invitation.

Resources are paper, six suitable passages and volunteer preparation and access support. Do not track which piles diminish, record choices or retain reading histories. Keep temporary delivery details only as needed. The chief limits are labels that feel patronizing, unsuitable selections and the additional preparation compared with a plain shelf.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: In each pilot set, make the same passages available through both the intention headings and a plain contents sheet containing only titles and brief neutral descriptions. During optional check-ins, ask which entry point makes choosing easier and whether the headings fit the readings. Do not record individual selections or compare category popularity. Check that preparing three options is sustainable and that residents receiving oral access can choose without explaining themselves. If the neutral contents sheet works as well, or the headings constrain expectations or feel intrusive, retain the simpler presentation. Record only operational findings and feedback that cannot identify a lone participant.

EXPAND.title: Build a tiny anthology together
EXPAND.proposal:
Residents assemble a shared reading object from independently enjoyable fragments. Each fortnight, a volunteer selects three short public-domain pieces around a concrete theme, such as windows or weather. Each piece fits on one sheet and makes sense alone. Residents may read any sheet, then fold a copy into a communal anthology on the lobby shelf. Reading without adding a page is equally welcome. At the fortnight’s end, the volunteer supplies missing pages and makes the completed anthology available for the next cycle.

The mechanism is collective construction: a visible, usable object gives a small contribution a shared consequence. It could work with one resident because the volunteer completes the object; additional readers are welcome rather than necessary. Unlike a response board, it asks for no personal writing or disclosure. Its prerequisites are suitable short texts, paper that can be folded into a booklet, and a volunteer able to maintain a clearly labelled assembly example. Its limit is that assembly might attract attention without deepening reading or connection.

Use week one to prepare the pieces, demonstrate folding and confirm accessible participation. Pilot during weeks two and three, completing one anthology each week; use week four to simplify or repeat. Through consented volunteer check-ins, residents unable to reach or stand at the shelf can receive every piece, hear it read aloud, and ask the volunteer to add a page on their behalf. Establish a seated, announced volunteer contact opportunity for requesting this help without a directory.

Keep contributions unmarked, collect no names or reading histories, and retain only the finished texts. No purchases are needed. Invitations must explicitly welcome taking a complete copy without contributing.
EXPAND.experiment: During each pilot week, also offer the same pieces as a ready-made packet. Ask willing readers whether helping assemble the shared version added any satisfaction or sense of participation. Record only anonymous feedback themes and whether assembly and requested accessible delivery worked. Do not interpret missing pages as evidence that nobody read. If readers prefer the packet and describe assembly as confusing or pointless in both weeks, the construction mechanism has not justified its upkeep.

EXPAND.title: Readers choose the next doorway
EXPAND.proposal:
Give residents a small but consequential editorial decision each week. A volunteer offers two brief public-domain excerpts, each followed by a description of the complete short text it comes from. Residents may fold an unmarked paper slip to choose which complete text appears the following week. Publish both texts if the choice is tied; if nobody chooses, use a stated default. Keep the unselected text available on request.

The mechanism is shared agency: residents shape what the building reads next instead of receiving a fixed programme. Even one choice changes the next offering, so a small turnout can sustain the ritual. The choice is between texts, never between residents, and no vote totals, winners’ table or participation ranking appear. It assumes the committee can prepare two suitable options and honour the choice promptly. Choice may encourage return visits, but this is uncertain; a ballot can also feel like unnecessary administration.

In week one, prepare three pairs of excerpts and their complete texts, plus folded paper voting instructions. During the two-week pilot in weeks two and three, each release includes the text selected previously and the next pair of excerpts. Week four honours the final pilot choice and reviews whether to continue. This requires paper, shelf space and a weekly volunteer check.

Residents unable to stand at or reach the shelf can receive or hear the options during consented volunteer check-ins and return an unmarked folded slip through the volunteer. Announce a seated contact opportunity to arrange this without a directory. Volunteers must not record who selected what. Mix slips before counting, retain only the resulting editorial choice, and discard the slips immediately. Participation, voting and future contact remain optional; reading never requires a vote or purchase.
EXPAND.experiment: Across the two pilot weeks, present one reader-selected text and one comparably short volunteer-selected text with equal prominence. Invite optional feedback on whether having a say made anyone more interested in the next release. Inspect whether choices were honoured on time and accessible requests were fulfilled; keep only operational notes and unattributed themes. Selection counts cannot establish readership. If willing readers report no value from choosing, or the process repeatedly confuses them, use straightforward volunteer selection instead.

EXPAND.title: Carry a line into the building
EXPAND.proposal:
Make reading a recurring invitation to notice a familiar place differently. Each week, offer one complete, very short public-domain text and a voluntary observation cue tied to it: after a poem about light, for example, notice changing light from wherever you normally sit. The following week, a small paper marker beside the new text names the previous cue, giving neighbours an easy opening for conversation without asking anyone to report an experience.

The mechanism is transfer from words to everyday attention. A text becomes connected to something residents may encounter repeatedly between readings, potentially creating common ground even when they never attend together. This differs from collecting interpretations: observations stay private unless residents choose to talk. It assumes the available texts support simple sensory or reflective cues. The committee must choose cues that can be done seated, indoors and without seeing, hearing, moving or leaving home being mandatory; offer an imagined or remembered alternative each time. The main uncertainty is whether noticing actually creates shared connection rather than merely a pleasant individual activity.

Use week one to select two texts and check the cues with a willing resident for clarity and accessibility. Run one text-and-cue cycle in each of weeks two and three. In week four, retain only cues residents found worthwhile. Paper copies and volunteer read-alouds require no purchases. Consented check-ins provide delivery and conversation for residents unable to reach or stand at the shelf; an announced seated volunteer contact opportunity allows requests without a resident directory.

Keep no observation sheets, attributed comments, attendance lists or reading histories. Do not ask residents to watch neighbours, enter private spaces or disclose personal memories. Reading alone, ignoring the cue and declining conversation are all valid choices.
EXPAND.experiment: Each pilot text should be usable without its separately folded observation cue. At optional check-ins, ask whether trying the cue changed how the text stayed with the reader, and whether it supplied a comfortable conversation opening compared with simply reading. Record only broad feedback themes and accessibility problems. Do not infer connection from copies taken. If cues feel burdensome or inaccessible, or willing readers describe no added value across both weeks, remove them and retain the plain reading offer.

EXPAND.title: Solve a small text mystery together
EXPAND.proposal:
Offer a weekly reading puzzle: a complete public-domain short text with three numbered gaps, followed by the three missing passages in mixed order. Residents match passages to gaps using clues in the language. Choose passages whose order can reasonably be inferred, and provide a folded answer sheet containing the intact text and a brief explanation. Readers may open it immediately; solving is optional.

The mechanism is a shared, bounded problem. Looking for connections gives residents a concrete reason to reread and something specific to discuss: “What made you put that passage there?” Unlike assembling a physical anthology, the useful work is interpreting relationships within the writing. One resident can solve independently or compare reasoning with a volunteer during a consented check-in; simultaneous attendance is unnecessary. No answers, scores or completion records are collected or displayed.

Use week one to prepare two puzzles and have a volunteer check that each is understandable and has a defensible solution. Run one puzzle in each of weeks two and three. During week four, review whether the activity merits repeating. Supplies are paper, donated texts, shelf space and volunteer preparation and check-in time. Label puzzles as playful invitations, with the complete text equally available to anyone who prefers ordinary reading.

Offer large, clearly spaced copies and delivery or individual read-alouds through consented volunteer check-ins. A shelf notice should invite residents who see it to pass the invitation verbally, helping residents who cannot reach or stand at the shelf learn about the offer. Volunteers arrange requested help directly without creating a directory or retaining reading histories. Reach remains uncertain where residents have neither existing check-ins nor neighbour contact.

The main limits are preparation effort, ambiguity and the possibility that a puzzle feels like schoolwork rather than shared pleasure.
EXPAND.experiment: During the two-week pilot, offer the puzzle and an intact copy of the same text with a simple discussion question. At optional check-ins, ask which format made it easier to begin or sustain a conversation, and whether the puzzle felt frustrating. Keep only aggregate format preferences and preparation time, without names or individual answers. A minimal positive signal is one resident finding the puzzle a useful conversation starter and volunteers being able to prepare both weeks reliably. If willing testers consistently prefer the intact version, cannot understand the puzzle, or discuss only answer correctness, the added mechanism has not earned its effort. With very few responses, report feasibility only; copy uptake cannot establish engagement.

If neither week produces reciprocal engagement, or residents avoid the sheet because of exposure concerns, the mechanism has not justified its extra work.

REFINE.title: The next instalment belongs to next week
REFINE.proposal:
Turn a short public-domain story into a recurring two-part reading. Each fortnight, residents receive the first half in week one and the conclusion in week two. Choose a text with a natural break and label the release dates clearly. Include a short recap with the conclusion so residents can join late. Offer one optional prompt before the ending arrives: “What do you think happens next?” Residents can consider it privately or discuss it during a volunteer check-in; no predictions are collected or scored.

The mechanism is narrative anticipation. An unfinished story supplies a reason to return, while a common release rhythm gives even two neighbours an easy conversation starter. Unlike a discussion meeting, the ritual does not depend on residents attending together. It assumes the committee can find a short, readable story whose division feels enjoyable rather than frustrating. State its approximate reading time. Residents who prefer the complete story may request both halves immediately; the weekly rhythm must never become a condition of access.

Use week one of the committee’s four weeks to select and prepare a story and confirm accessible distribution. Run its two instalments during weeks two and three, then decide in week four whether to repeat fortnightly. Put paper copies on the shelf and offer delivery or read-aloud versions through consented volunteer check-ins for residents unable to stand there. Volunteers keep no records of reading progress or predictions; any temporary delivery instructions are discarded after use. Resources are two paper batches, a short recap and volunteer availability. The main limits are unsuitable story breaks, memory demands and residents simply preferring complete texts.
REFINE.experiment: During the two-week pilot, make a complete-story packet available alongside the dated instalments. At optional check-ins, ask whether waiting for the ending created pleasant anticipation, caused frustration or made no difference compared with receiving the whole story. Inspect whether the second instalment was released reliably and whether residents joining in week two could follow it using the recap. Record only aggregate operational observations and unattributed feedback themes. If willing readers consistently prefer the complete packet, or the recap does not support late entry, abandon serial release and use complete texts.

REFINE.title: Pass the editor’s turn
REFINE.proposal:
Give residents a small, consequential editorial role: choosing what the building reads next. Each week, a volunteer prepares two donated public-domain passages, each complete and short enough to read in about five minutes. An optional resident editor chooses one and gives it a text-focused invitation, such as “Read this for its surprising last sentence.” The volunteer prints that invitation with the passage. Everyone may read privately, discuss it during a consented check-in, or simply take a copy. No meeting or written response is required.

The mechanism is shared ownership: a neighbour’s editorial choice gives an otherwise ordinary shelf text a local reason to be read. One willing resident can sustain the role with volunteer support; if nobody chooses, the volunteer supplies the next selection. Editors may repeat, and residents need never disclose their role publicly. This assumes someone enjoys choosing and that volunteers can offer two genuinely accessible options. It may fail if choosing feels like homework or volunteer selections dominate.

Use week one to prepare four candidate passages and a paper invitation explaining how to request an editorial turn through a volunteer check-in. Run the two-week pilot in weeks two and three; use week four to revise or stop. Provide large, clear print and offer delivery, oral presentation of the choices, and read-aloud access through explicitly consented check-ins. Confirm a workable request route for residents unable to reach or stand at the shelf before launch.

Keep no editor roster, reading histories, names on passages, or public tally. Invitations must avoid personal anecdotes that identify the chooser. Volunteers retain delivery instructions only as long as needed. Resources are paper, shelf space, prepared texts and brief volunteer visits; no purchases, directory or app are needed.
REFINE.experiment: In each pilot week, offer the resident-selected passage beside an equally short volunteer-selected passage, clearly labelled by selection method without naming anyone. Reverse their shelf positions in week two. During optional check-ins, ask whether the neighbour’s choice supplied any extra reason to read and whether choosing felt enjoyable or burdensome. Do not track who takes either passage or link feedback across weeks. Record only whether selection and accessible distribution happened, plus broad feedback themes; suppress details that could identify a lone participant. The mechanism lacks support if nobody wants an editorial turn, choosing creates pressure, or willing readers find the neighbour-selected invitation adds nothing over the ordinary selection. Two weeks can establish feasibility, not lasting participation.

REFINE.title: One passage, one weekly pause—with a reachable invitation
REFINE.proposal:
Repair original candidate 0, the strongest fit because a shared weekly passage works with one reader and requires little coordination. Exact weakness: its accessible delivery depends on existing check-ins, while residents unable to reach the shelf may have no way to discover or request them. Changed action: during preparation week, volunteers make one building-wide doorstep invitation round, offering a paper invitation and briefly explaining the optional delivery/read-aloud service wherever someone answers. No response means no further visit. Residents may explicitly request passage delivery at an agreed time for the two pilot weeks; volunteers retain only temporary delivery instructions, never reading progress, and discard them after the pilot. This makes the access route concrete without creating a directory or requiring a shelf visit.

Preserve the ritual: in weeks two and three, release one complete, short public-domain passage each Monday and hold a ten-minute weekly reading pause in a confirmed seated location. Reading privately or hearing the passage during a consented visit also counts; comments and attendance are optional. A volunteer keeps the appointment even for one participant. No purchases, app, names, attendance lists, public rankings or identifiable reading histories. Prerequisites are permitted doorstep access, an accessible seated location, clear-print copies and volunteers able to honour requested visits. In week four, revise and decide whether to repeat. Remaining limit: residents unavailable during the invitation round may still be missed.
REFINE.experiment: Run the two-week pilot without the original extra comparator text. Keep only operational checks: whether both passages and pauses happened, whether every requested delivery/read-aloud was fulfilled, and whether volunteer time stayed within a limit set in preparation week. Collect no participant counts or individual feedback records. At a consented delivery, optionally ask whether the resident can use this arrangement again; retain only a general access problem requiring correction. The smallest falsifying check is one requested visit that cannot be fulfilled: that disproves the proposed access arrangement’s feasibility and must be repaired before repeating it. Two weeks establishes delivery feasibility, not lasting social benefit.

SAVE.title: One passage, one weekly pause
SAVE.proposal:
Make one short passage the building’s shared weekly reference point. Each Monday, volunteers place paper copies of a donated public-domain text on the lobby shelf, with one optional question such as “Which image stayed with you?” Residents can read whenever they wish. At a fixed weekly time, a volunteer offers a ten-minute read-aloud and conversation; one resident and one volunteer are enough, and silence is welcome. Reading alone still counts as participating.

The mechanism is a predictable shared focus: residents can encounter the same words without coordinating schedules or finishing a book. It assumes a volunteer can keep the appointment and that at least one suitable seated location is available. For residents unable to reach or stand at the shelf, volunteers offer paper delivery or an individual read-aloud during existing, consented check-ins. The committee must confirm this access route before launching; it cannot assume every resident already receives visits.

Use the first week to choose four short texts, prepare a plain-language invitation and confirm accessibility. Pilot during weeks two and three; use week four to adjust the routine. Invitations should say that attendance, comments and future contact are optional. Keep no names, quotations attributed to residents, attendance lists or records of who reads which text. Any temporary delivery arrangements stay with the volunteer and are discarded when no longer needed. This requires paper, shelf space and dependable volunteer time. Its limit is that a shared passage may create familiarity without producing conversation.
SAVE.experiment: For the two-week pilot, offer one passage and one scheduled pause each week. Also leave an equally short, unprompted public-domain text available as a simple shelf-only comparator. At optional check-ins, ask whether the scheduled shared passage gave residents a reason to read or connect that the unprompted text did not. Record only broad operational findings, without linking answers across weeks. Check that copies and read-aloud access reached anyone requesting them, and that the appointment happened even with one participant. If residents find the schedule burdensome or see no additional value, retain the simpler shelf-only option.

SAVE.title: A paper conversation that waits for you
SAVE.proposal:
Create a weekly conversation carried by paper rather than simultaneous attendance. Put copies of one short public-domain text on the shelf alongside a folded response sheet. Its outside carries one concrete prompt; inside, residents may leave an unsigned sentence, a drawing or a question. A volunteer checks the sheet midweek and adds a response grounded in the text when needed, so a single resident can receive an answer. At week’s end, the volunteer places a brief, unattributed recap beside the next text.

The mechanism is delayed reciprocity: someone encounters a previous response and can answer it without meeting its author. It assumes residents are comfortable with contributions being visible to neighbours and that a volunteer can moderate twice weekly. Do not promise anonymity: handwriting or personal anecdotes may identify someone. Invite text-focused contributions, discourage personal details, and state that identifying or hurtful material will be removed. Do not copy or archive original sheets; discard them after the weekly recap. Participation requires neither a contribution nor a purchase.

During week one, prepare two texts, response sheets and the privacy notice. Run the pilot in weeks two and three, then revise in week four. Residents unable to stand at or reach the shelf can receive copies through consented volunteer check-ins, dictate a text-focused response for transcription, and hear the previous contributions read aloud. Volunteers must obtain permission before sharing dictated words. No directory or ongoing reader profiles are created. This needs paper, pencils and a volunteer willing to respond and moderate. Its limits are possible reluctance to write publicly and the risk that volunteer contributions dominate.
SAVE.experiment: In each pilot week, offer the conversation sheet alongside an ordinary take-away copy of the same text. Inspect whether any resident contribution receives a relevant reply, including a volunteer reply, and whether later contributions engage with earlier ones. Keep only a weekly aggregate description, not individual records or handwriting samples. Ask willing participants whether reading others’ responses added anything beyond the plain copy and whether privacy felt adequate. If neither week produces reciprocal engagement, or residents avoid the sheet because of exposure concerns, the mechanism has not justified its extra work.

Run its two instalments during weeks two and three, then decide in week four whether to repeat fortnightly. SAVE.title: Build a tiny anthology together
SAVE.proposal:
Residents assemble a shared reading object from independently enjoyable fragments. Each fortnight, a volunteer selects three short public-domain pieces around a concrete theme, such as windows or weather. Each piece fits on one sheet and makes sense alone. Residents may read any sheet, then fold a copy into a communal anthology on the lobby shelf. Reading without adding a page is equally welcome. At the fortnight’s end, the volunteer supplies missing pages and makes the completed anthology available for the next cycle.

The mechanism is collective construction: a visible, usable object gives a small contribution a shared consequence. It could work with one resident because the volunteer completes the object; additional readers are welcome rather than necessary. Unlike a response board, it asks for no personal writing or disclosure. Its prerequisites are suitable short texts, paper that can be folded into a booklet, and a volunteer able to maintain a clearly labelled assembly example. Its limit is that assembly might attract attention without deepening reading or connection.

Use week one to prepare the pieces, demonstrate folding and confirm accessible participation. Pilot during weeks two and three, completing one anthology each week; use week four to simplify or repeat. Through consented volunteer check-ins, residents unable to reach or stand at the shelf can receive every piece, hear it read aloud, and ask the volunteer to add a page on their behalf. Establish a seated, announced volunteer contact opportunity for requesting this help without a directory.

Keep contributions unmarked, collect no names or reading histories, and retain only the finished texts. No purchases are needed. Invitations must explicitly welcome taking a complete copy without contributing.
SAVE.experiment: During each pilot week, also offer the same pieces as a ready-made packet. Ask willing readers whether helping assemble the shared version added any satisfaction or sense of participation. Record only anonymous feedback themes and whether assembly and requested accessible delivery worked. Do not interpret missing pages as evidence that nobody read. If readers prefer the packet and describe assembly as confusing or pointless in both weeks, the construction mechanism has not justified its upkeep.

SAVE.title: Readers choose the next doorway
SAVE.proposal:
Give residents a small but consequential editorial decision each week. A volunteer offers two brief public-domain excerpts, each followed by a description of the complete short text it comes from. Residents may fold an unmarked paper slip to choose which complete text appears the following week. Publish both texts if the choice is tied; if nobody chooses, use a stated default. Keep the unselected text available on request.

The mechanism is shared agency: residents shape what the building reads next instead of receiving a fixed programme. Even one choice changes the next offering, so a small turnout can sustain the ritual. The choice is between texts, never between residents, and no vote totals, winners’ table or participation ranking appear. It assumes the committee can prepare two suitable options and honour the choice promptly. Choice may encourage return visits, but this is uncertain; a ballot can also feel like unnecessary administration.

In week one, prepare three pairs of excerpts and their complete texts, plus folded paper voting instructions. During the two-week pilot in weeks two and three, each release includes the text selected previously and the next pair of excerpts. Week four honours the final pilot choice and reviews whether to continue. This requires paper, shelf space and a weekly volunteer check.

Residents unable to stand at or reach the shelf can receive or hear the options during consented volunteer check-ins and return an unmarked folded slip through the volunteer. Announce a seated contact opportunity to arrange this without a directory. Volunteers must not record who selected what. Mix slips before counting, retain only the resulting editorial choice, and discard the slips immediately. Participation, voting and future contact remain optional; reading never requires a vote or purchase.
SAVE.experiment: Across the two pilot weeks, present one reader-selected text and one comparably short volunteer-selected text with equal prominence. Invite optional feedback on whether having a say made anyone more interested in the next release. Inspect whether choices were honoured on time and accessible requests were fulfilled; keep only operational notes and unattributed themes. Selection counts cannot establish readership. If willing readers report no value from choosing, or the process repeatedly confuses them, use straightforward volunteer selection instead.

SAVE.title: Carry a line into the building
SAVE.proposal:
Make reading a recurring invitation to notice a familiar place differently. Each week, offer one complete, very short public-domain text and a voluntary observation cue tied to it: after a poem about light, for example, notice changing light from wherever you normally sit. The following week, a small paper marker beside the new text names the previous cue, giving neighbours an easy opening for conversation without asking anyone to report an experience.

The mechanism is transfer from words to everyday attention. A text becomes connected to something residents may encounter repeatedly between readings, potentially creating common ground even when they never attend together. This differs from collecting interpretations: observations stay private unless residents choose to talk. It assumes the available texts support simple sensory or reflective cues. The committee must choose cues that can be done seated, indoors and without seeing, hearing, moving or leaving home being mandatory; offer an imagined or remembered alternative each time. The main uncertainty is whether noticing actually creates shared connection rather than merely a pleasant individual activity.

Use week one to select two texts and check the cues with a willing resident for clarity and accessibility. Run one text-and-cue cycle in each of weeks two and three. In week four, retain only cues residents found worthwhile. Paper copies and volunteer read-alouds require no purchases. Consented check-ins provide delivery and conversation for residents unable to reach or stand at the shelf; an announced seated volunteer contact opportunity allows requests without a resident directory.

Keep no observation sheets, attributed comments, attendance lists or reading histories. Do not ask residents to watch neighbours, enter private spaces or disclose personal memories. Reading alone, ignoring the cue and declining conversation are all valid choices.
SAVE.experiment: Each pilot text should be usable without its separately folded observation cue. At optional check-ins, ask whether trying the cue changed how the text stayed with the reader, and whether it supplied a comfortable conversation opening compared with simply reading. Record only broad feedback themes and accessibility problems. Do not infer connection from copies taken. If cues feel burdensome or inaccessible, or willing readers describe no added value across both weeks, remove them and retain the plain reading offer.
